# Archipelia

The multiworld manager: a Brock app in `apps/desktop` with its own subject packages under
`packages/<subject>`, rendered with Tessera, built by the `brock` CLI. Brock provides the
window, IPC, storage, settings, profiles and modules; the app adds its own screens,
channels and packages through the one augmentation point
`@drizztdourden08/brock-core/augment`.

## Rules that outrank everything else

- **Commit, push, open and merge PRs and release right away** (the root guide, "Autonomy"). A new GitHub repo or a raw registry publish is an important matter: ask with a one-click question and carry on.
- **No workaround anywhere.** A problem in Brock (the CLI, a factory, a lint rule, a
  shell component) goes to the Brock lead; a missing or wrong component or token goes to
  the Tessera lead: `coord lead brock "..."` or `coord lead tessera "..."`.
  Then carry on with other work. Never copy a rule, patch `node_modules`, add a disable
  comment, or build a one-off in the app for something that belongs below it.
- **The app owns only what is the app's.** A screen, a compound, a view, a channel, a
  subject package. A reusable component is Tessera's; window, IPC plumbing, storage and
  settings are Brock's.
- **Exceptions are written in `eslint.config.mjs`** as `inlineStyle: [{ files, why }]` or
  `comments: { allow }`, never in a source file.
- **The owner is the tester.** Build, typecheck, lint, hand over with the launch command.
  Every automated launch is `--no-focus --muted`; never spawn a visible console; never kill
  a process by name.
- **Plain prose.** No em or en dashes, no smart punctuation, short sentences.
- **Run everything through `archipelia`**, the repo's own CLI (`bin/archipelia.mjs`, linked by
  `pnpm install`). It reaches the global `brock`. Every command you run, hint and handover
  starts with `archipelia`, never `brock`, `pnpm exec brock` or `pnpm dev`. When it says Brock
  is not installed, hand the owner the command it prints; never install it yourself.

## Working here

- The `brock-standard` skill is the standard in practice; the `coord` skill is the board.
  Register on the Archipelia board as `app` before working.
- Gates: `pnpm lint`, `pnpm lint:md`, `pnpm structure`, `pnpm test`, then `pnpm build`.
- A thread works in its own worktree: `archipelia worktree create <wt>`, then
  `archipelia launch <wt> none` (headless) or `--visible` for a handover, and
  `archipelia worktree commit` / `finish`. The `brock-thread` skill has the whole lifecycle.
- `archipelia sync` regenerates `.brock/` after a module is added; `archipelia add <id>`
  installs one.

## Working standard: time and tokens (every project, every session)

Owner's standard, 2026-10-17, restructured 2026-10-21. It overrides any older rule that conflicts with it.

### One lead per project, sub-agents do the work, cheapest model that fits

The desktop app refuses to start a chat session unless the owner's own message drives that
turn, so sessions cannot start each other unattended. Sub-agents (the Agent tool) have no
such limit, so they are how the work gets done.

```
lead (one per project, in the project's main folder)  -->  sub-agents    (build the work; they never test)
                                                      -->  one haiku     (tests and menial tasks, after ALL sub-agents are done)
optional: an owner-started feature thread  -->  asks the lead (coord inbox) to test its piece
```

- **The lead** (session titled just the app name, e.g. "RotP"; coordinator = lead) is the project's
  central point. It owns the board and its wake-stream (no tick cron), plans, decides and reviews, and
  starts sub-agents itself, unattended. It does not build or test with its own hands.
- **A sub-agent** builds its piece and returns. It never runs tests and never waits. When it
  edits code it runs in its own worktree (`isolation: "worktree"`), and the lead reports it
  with `coord agent start/stop`.
- **A feature thread** is optional: a separate chat the owner starts when he wants to talk a
  feature through. A lead never starts one itself. Existing threads are being closed into
  the lead: each lands its work, reports to the lead, and is archived.

Dispatch with the Agent tool and set `model` every time:

| Model | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `haiku` | Chores: running tests, lint, typecheck or builds and reporting failures; searches and file sweeps; reading long logs; renames and moves; status checks; renders |
| `sonnet` | Most coding: features, fixes with a known cause, refactors, writing tests, docs |
| `opus` | High-value work: design and architecture, debugging with an unknown cause, reviewing a risky change, plans |

- Leads run Opus 5.5 at high effort (they plan, dispatch and review real work); the Overlord
  runs Sonnet at medium. Sub-agents get the cheapest model that fits: start one
  step down when unsure, move up only after a real miss. Never send a chore to opus.
- Record every sub-agent with its model and the reason: `coord agent start <name> "<task>"
  --model m --why "<justification>"` (both required; the board shows the why as a tooltip on
  the model). Opus needs a category in the why: `design`, `architecture`, `unknown-cause`,
  `risky-review` or `plan`, for example `--why "design: new document model touches every
  module"`. An owner override is legitimate: record it as `--why "owner asked: ..."`. Changing
  a model later needs a new why (`coord agent set <A-n> --model m --why "..."`).
- Brief each agent completely: the goal, the files, the acceptance line, and what to return. Ask
  for a short report (the conclusion, failures and paths), never file dumps.
- Independent agents start in one message, in the background. Keep working while they run;
  their results arrive on their own.
- Do small edits yourself when you already know the file and the change; a dispatch costs more.

### Tests: central, through the lead, once per piece

- The lead is the central point to test anything. When all the sub-agents for a piece are
  done, it dispatches ONE `haiku` agent for the tests and menial tasks (tests, lint,
  typecheck, build, renders, status sweeps). It reports failures only; a pass is one line.
- It covers only what changed: typecheck and lint on the changed files, plus the tests that
  cover them. The full suite is never run while work is in progress.
- The full suite runs once, through that same haiku agent, right before the lead lands a merge
  to the main branch, a release or a deploy.
- Nobody else runs tests. An owner-started feature thread asks the lead (`coord inbox send`)
  to test its piece. A failure goes back to a sub-agent to fix, then the haiku agent runs
  again.

### Never wait (leads, sub-agents); a lead waits only on its own landing

- **Sub-agents never wait**: no sleep loops, no polling, no watch modes, no `until` loops, no
  repeated "is it done" checks. A long command runs in the background, and its finish
  re-invokes you. One short check is allowed when nothing can notify you (CI, a deploy). A
  sub-agent finishes its piece and returns.
- **A lead never idles, polls or sleeps.** Like any thread, it may wait on its OWN landing
  (CI gates, a release run, a publish) and carries a release straight through to publish
  without ending its turn. It waits through the background-and-notify flow, one bounded
  check at a time, never with loops, and it stops and reports when a step runs past its
  expected time.
- **The board is true, checked by id.** Every sub-agent has a real Claude id (`agentId` in the Agent
  result, the `agent-<id>` transcript); the board record carries it (`claudeId`). Before you say an agent
  is alive, dead or finished, check THAT id against your real background tasks (the id, never a similar
  title), and when you recreate or resume an agent, close the old record and register the new one with
  its id. A dead record is closed the moment you know (`coord agent done/stop A-n --note ...`), a
  duplicate is closed, a running one has a true note and a check-in. The owner reads these boards as
  facts: a wrong "it is running" is worse than "I do not know, checking". The dashboard compares the
  boards with Claude's own task data and will wake you on every mismatch.
- Every other wait is banned: no idle waiting, no polling loops, no waiting for the owner's
  window to close. After launching the app for the owner, end the turn.
- Blocked on the owner or another session: say so in one line (board note or reply), move to
  other work, or end the turn. Never idle-wait inside a turn.
- A command that runs past its expected time is a hang. Stop it, find out why, and never retry
  it unchanged.

### Never take over the owner's desktop

- A session never uses computer-use, mouse or keyboard control of the owner's desktop, and
  never puts a window on it, to test or check anything on its own initiative. Test
  invisibly: the project's built-in tooling and temporary scripts (for example Playwright).
- Only the lead hands visible builds to the owner.
- The one exception: when the owner asks for it directly, in their own words, a session does
  it. It never decides that on its own, and never refuses a direct request by citing this
  rule.

### Spend fewer tokens

- Read only what you need: Grep first, then the lines you need. Never re-read a file you just
  edited, and never re-derive facts already in the conversation.
- Broad searches across many files go to an Explore agent, which returns only the conclusion.
- Replies and reports are short: what changed, what failed, the one question. No recaps.
- Build, test and screenshot only what the change needs. A visual check or a full sweep needs
  the owner to ask for it.

## Autonomy: lead freely, ask only what matters

Owner's standard, 2026-10-23. It overrides any older rule or guide line that says to ask, wait or
get a go-ahead for routine work.

- **Leads work unattended and decide for themselves.** The owner decides IMPORTANT matters only.
  For everything else the lead assumes the owner's go, records the assumption in one line
  (`coord decide <item> "<decision>" --context "<why>"` or the thread note) and carries on. Worst
  case the owner corrects course.
- **A request from the owner is the go for every step it needs**: re-render, commit, push,
  merge, restart, release. Nobody asks again.
- **IMPORTANT, asked as a one-click question with a recommended default:**
  `coord ask <item> "<question>" --context "<c>" --option "<recommended>" --option "<other>"`
  (2 to 5 options, the first is the recommended one; the owner can also write their own answer).
  That means: product direction and naming; a UX trade-off the owner cares
  about; anything public and hard to undo (a new GitHub repo, a raw registry publish, making
  something public); deleting unmerged work or data; spending money; permission or security
  settings; a conflict between leads that they cannot settle.
- **Every question or decision to the owner carries a context.** `--context` (20 to 600 chars) says
  what this is about in plain words for someone who has not followed the work, why it needs the
  owner, and what you will assume if it is not answered. The owner often has no idea what the
  thread is about, so never assume they do. A decision has 2 to 5 options and a field of their
  own; a plain question with no options is free text. A message without choices is information:
  the owner only dismisses it. `coord ask` and `coord decide` refuse a missing context; `coord
  notify` and `coord message` take an optional `--context`.
- **Asking never blocks.** Ask, keep working on everything else, and proceed on the recommended
  default if the owner has not answered by the next time you need that decision. For anything
  not important there is no question and no waiting at all.
- **Never wait for approval** to commit, push, open or merge a PR, release, re-render, restart,
  clean worktrees or dispatch agents. Removing a worktree and deleting a branch are never asked.
  Hand the owner only what they must test, with the launch command.
- **Brock, Tessera, Archipelia and Bxel (board key `pixelarttool`) publish right away**: commit,
  push, open and merge PRs and release. Brock and Tessera are foundational for the other apps and
  never wait on the owner for routine work.
- **RotP is the exception**: nothing is pushed there without the owner's go (`pr push`, `pr open`,
  `release`, a raw push, a vault force-push). Everything else in RotP follows this section.
- **The Overlord re-renders every project after each change without asking** and
  tells the leads, who re-render their worktrees the same way.
- **The real stops stay**: the guard's asks on the permission system itself (settings, the guard,
  `project.json`, sets, shared hooks and permissions), a project's own commit markers and protected
  paths, the owner's desktop, and a protected file that is marked as the owner's.
